01 / THE QUESTION

Privacy depends on context.

Personal agents can read images, draft messages, and act on our behalf. Recognizing sensitive information is only part of the challenge: they must also decide when sharing it is appropriate.

MPCI-Bench tests both sides of that decision. Each pair uses the same source image in two contrasting social contexts, assessing whether an agent can protect privacy while still completing legitimate tasks.

02 / THE BENCHMARK

From knowing the norm
to taking the right action.

Three tiers connect abstract privacy judgments to the decisions an agent makes with tools.

NORMATIVE JUDGMENT

Who can share what with whom?

Structured contextual-integrity parameters describe the data subject, sender, recipient, data type, and transmission principle. Paired seeds contrast an appropriate flow with an inappropriate one.

INPUT

Source image + structured CI parameters

WHAT IT TESTS

Recognition of contextual privacy norms

Built with quality at each stage

Tri-Principle Iterative Refinement checks semantic utility, contextual appropriateness, and story realism. Both sides of a pair must pass the quality filter before trace simulation.

03 / KEY FINDINGS

Knowing privacy norms
doesn’t guarantee private actions.

In the paper’s action evaluation, visual information is leaked more often than text. Strong probing performance does not reliably translate into safe tool use.

01

A gap between judgment and action

Models can identify inappropriate flows in a direct question yet still disclose sensitive information when completing the corresponding agent task.

02

Images are a blind spot

Visual leakage exceeds textual leakage across every evaluated model. Direct image attachment is a major source of disclosure.

03

Refusal alone isn’t enough

Privacy safeguards must preserve useful sharing in appropriate contexts. The paired design exposes the cost of overly conservative behavior.

PRIVACY + UTILITY

Context-aware filtering shows promise.

For Mistral-Large-3, the CI Filter reduces visual leakage while retaining high utility on appropriate flows.

Prompt-based intervention; Table 5, arXiv v3. Results are specific to the evaluated model and setup.

Evaluation scope and limitations

The benchmark uses synthetic stories and simulated agent traces grounded in VISPR images. Contextual norms may vary across cultures and domains. Automated action evaluation uses an LLM judge; the human study validates story quality, not every action outcome. These findings describe the models and setup in the January 2026 arXiv version.
